lesson.title: A TLS 1.3 Handshake, Message by Message
lesson.summary: The TLS 1.3 handshake is the brief exchange at the start of a connection where client and server agree on a cipher suite, the server proves its identity with its certificate, and both sides derive the symmetric keys that protect everything that follows, all within a single round trip.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters described TLS's hybrid design in general terms: authenticate the server and agree on a key using public key cryptography and certificates, then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data. This chapter walks through exactly how that happens, message by message, in TLS 1.3, the version specified in RFC 8446 that streamlined the handshake down to what is usually called one round trip, or 1-RTT, meaning encrypted application data can start flowing after a single round trip between client and server.

The exchange begins with the client sending a ClientHello. This message proposes a TLS version, lists the cipher suites the client supports in preference order, includes a random nonce, and, this is the change that let TLS 1.3 collapse the handshake down from TLS 1.2's extra round trip, includes a key_share extension: an ephemeral public key value for one or more key exchange groups, such as the elliptic curve X25519, that the client is guessing the server will be willing to use. Sending this eagerly, before the server has even confirmed it will accept that group, is what saves a round trip compared to asking first and exchanging key material second.

The server responds with a ServerHello, choosing one cipher suite from the client's offered list, including its own random nonce, and including its own key_share, an ephemeral public key for the same group the client proposed. At this point, both sides have everything they need to independently compute the identical shared secret: each combines its own ephemeral private value with the other side's ephemeral public value, using elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, the exact key agreement mechanism described in the public key cryptography chapter, without the shared secret itself ever having crossed the network.

From that shared secret, both sides derive a set of handshake traffic keys, and everything the server sends from this point on is already symmetrically encrypted with them. That includes EncryptedExtensions, carrying additional negotiated parameters, the server's Certificate message, its full X.509 chain, ready for the client to validate up to a trusted root exactly as described in the certificate chapters, a CertificateVerify message, which is a digital signature made with the certificate's private key over a hash of the handshake transcript so far, proving the server genuinely holds the private key matching that certificate and not merely a copy of the public certificate file, and finally a Finished message, a message authentication code over the entire handshake transcript confirming to the client that the server derived the same keys it did.

The client then verifies the certificate chain against its trusted root store, verifies the CertificateVerify signature, and verifies the server's Finished value. Once all of that checks out, the client sends its own Finished message, confirming that it too derived matching keys, and both sides separately derive a further set of application traffic keys from the same shared secret. From here on, every request and response, the actual HTTP traffic in an HTTPS connection, is protected with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, using those application traffic keys, which is the exact handoff from asymmetric to symmetric cryptography promised back in the TLS protocol chapter.

This is why the handshake is described as 1-RTT: the client sends one flight, the ClientHello; the server answers with one flight containing everything through its Finished message; the client answers with its own Finished and can immediately begin sending encrypted application data in that same flight, so protected data is flowing after a single round trip. TLS 1.2 needed an additional round trip because its cipher and key exchange negotiation were not collapsed into the initial hello messages the way TLS 1.3's key_share extension allows. It is also worth knowing, as an aside rather than the core mechanism, that TLS 1.3 supports an even faster 0-RTT mode for resuming a connection with a server a client has already talked to recently, letting the client send some application data in its very first flight; because that early data can potentially be replayed by an attacker who captures and resends it, servers are deliberately conservative about what they will accept over 0-RTT, typically restricting it to requests that are safe to receive more than once.
